add_nodes.statement: Extract performance: how ultrasound amplitude and time affect phenolic recovery and antioxidant activity.
Extract recovery: phenolic content of the extract under the tested amplitude and time conditions.
Extract antioxidant activity: DPPH radical-scavenging activity of the extract under the tested amplitude and time conditions.
Film barrier properties: water vapor permeability and oxygen permeability of the films across the extract concentrations.
Film mechanical properties: tensile strength, elongation, and Young's modulus of the films across the extract concentrations.
Film optical properties: opacity, color, and light transmittance of the films across the extract concentrations.
Film thermal properties: melting temperature, crystallinity, and thermal stability of the films across the extract concentrations.
Film antioxidant properties: DPPH radical-scavenging activity and total phenolic content of the films across the extract concentrations.
Packaging performance: preservation of dried-shrimp quality, microbial load, and sensory scores during storage.
Film property tradeoffs: how changes in extract concentration affect barrier, mechanical, optical, thermal, and antioxidant properties together.
Barrier tradeoff: higher extract concentration reduces water vapor permeability but may also reduce mechanical strength.
Mechanical tradeoff: higher extract concentration increases tensile strength but may reduce elongation.
Optical tradeoff: higher extract concentration increases opacity but may reduce light transmittance.
Thermal tradeoff: higher extract concentration changes melting temperature and crystallinity.
Antioxidant tradeoff: higher extract concentration increases DPPH activity and total phenolic content.
Package comparison: dried shrimp packaged with extract-containing films versus the reference film on quality, microbial load, and sensory scores during storage.
Dried-shrimp quality: moisture, pH, total volatile base nitrogen, and thiobarbituric acid reactive substances during storage.
Dried-shrimp microbial load: total aerobic plate count and yeast and mold count during storage.
Dried-shrimp sensory scores: appearance, color, aroma, taste, and overall acceptability during storage.
Film degradation: mass loss and biodegradation rate of the films during storage.

aspect_assessments.assessment: The broad formulation-dependent conclusion is supported by the different endpoint patterns, but its wording obscures the pure-car-nosine-only increase in serum transaminases and the commercial-supplement-specific MDA and histological differences.
limitations: The pure-car-nosine-only increase is a tendency because the table marks no significant Car+P-versus-ConP difference.
The commercial-supplement-specific MDA and histological differences are not significant differences in every group.
aspect_assessments.rationale: Each observation reports a different endpoint comparison.
aspect_assessments.scope: Six groups of six mice at 24 h after a single 110 mg/kg oral paracetamol dose.

aspect_assessments.assessment: The commercial supplement lowered MDA versus ConP and was more successful than pure carnosine in reducing MDA, while pure carnosine's apparent LP reduction was not significant.
limitations: Exact figure values were not inspected.
aspect_assessments.rationale: o03 directly compares MDA across formulations.
aspect_assessments.scope: Liver homogenates at 24 h.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Qualitative centrilobular necrosis occurred in 60% of ConP, 40% of Car+P with smaller areas, and only rare focal areas in CarS+P.
limitations: Representative images were not inspected.
aspect_assessments.rationale: o04 is the histological comparison.
aspect_assessments.scope: 24 h H&E and PAS assessment.

aspect_assessments.assessment: CYP2E1-positive area was significantly lower in Car+P and CarS+P than in ConP, while pure carnosine alone lowered it numerically.
limitations: CYP2E1 was quantified by immunohistochemistry.
aspect_assessments.rationale: o05 reports the CYP2E1 comparison.
aspect_assessments.scope: Quantified immunohistochemistry at 24 h.

aspect_assessments.assessment: COX-2 staining was focal and centrilobular/perinecrotic after paracetamol, absent in Con, Car and CarS, and more limited near injury foci in Car+P and CarS+P.
limitations: The assay was descriptive.
aspect_assessments.rationale: o06 is the COX-2 observation.
aspect_assessments.scope: Descriptive immunohistochemistry at 24 h.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Iba1-positive cell counts did not differ significantly among groups.
limitations: The marker does not distinguish macrophage subpopulations or activation state.
aspect_assessments.rationale: o07 reports the macrophage abundance comparison.
aspect_assessments.scope: Five randomly selected 200× fields at 24 h.

aspect_assessments.assessment: No significant differences were found for urea, creatinine and uric acid.
limitations: The lower mean uric acid in Car+P was non-significant.
aspect_assessments.rationale: o08 reports the renal markers.
aspect_assessments.scope: Serum markers at 24 h.

findings.description: The broad formulation-dependent conclusion combines different endpoint-specific comparisons that should be kept separate.

add_nodes.statement: Serum biochemical endpoint: pure carnosine alone increased transaminases versus paracetamol-only control without a table-marked significant Car+P-versus-ConP difference, while the commercial supplement lowered CarS+P AST numerically and CarS+P AST versus Car was significant.

Liver-homogenate oxidative endpoint: the commercial supplement prevented the MDA increase versus ConP and was more successful than pure carnosine in reducing MDA, while pure carnosine's apparent LP reduction was not significant.
Histological endpoint: centrilobular necrosis occurred in 60% of ConP, 40% of Car+P with smaller areas, and only rare focal areas in CarS+P.
CYP2E1 endpoint: CYP2E1-positive area was significantly lower in Car+P and CarS+P than in ConP, while pure carnosine alone lowered it numerically.
Inflammatory endpoint: COX-2 staining was focal and centrilobular/perinecrotic after paracetamol, absent in Con, Car and CarS, and more limited near injury foci in Car+P and CarS+P.
Macrophage abundance endpoint: Iba1-positive cell counts did not differ significantly among groups.

proposed_updates.rationale: The decomposition keeps each endpoint and each formulation comparison explicit without changing the existing evidence or the broad formulation-dependent claim n07.

missing_design_information: Whether the same serum samples were used for both comparisons
needed_observations: ALT, AST, total bilirubin and direct bilirubin in ConP versus Car+P and CarS+P with the same statistical test
verification_needs.unresolved_question: Does the commercial supplement lower serum transaminases more than pure carnosine alone?
verification_needs.why_informative: It would show whether the pure-car-nosine-only increase is a real difference that the commercial supplement can overcome.

verification_needs.comparison_or_control: Compare the formulations at matched time points and endpoints.
missing_design_information: Whether the time course was measured beyond 24 h
needed_observations: Time-resolved serum and tissue endpoints
verification_needs.unresolved_question: Do the endpoint differences persist beyond 24 h?
verification_needs.why_informative: It would show whether the differences are transient or persistent.

The hydrogen-evolution assay already measures corrosion rate, while the EIS and LSV assays can measure transport and anodic current density, both of which change with coating composition. The chitosan-only coating needs its own structural characterization because o04's characterization is only for the composite coating. The verification needs the two coating formulations, the comparator groups, the timing, and the independent method that the authors do not supply.

The claim rests on an unsupported structural statement, a reversed Ni3+/defect-oxygen comparison, and one diffusion coefficient. I remove the claim and link the supported transport and kinetics parts to n05; the structure and Ni3+/defect-oxygen statements remain open questions.
</think>

n20 says that cryogenic processing reduces structural defects and improves nanotube alignment, enhancing carrier mobility. The observations do not measure carrier mobility. Raman ID/IG is nearly identical (1.26 vs 1.30), and CTEM shows open rough ends and reduced entanglement. SEM shows less agglomeration. The photocurrent advantage (o17) is an optoelectronic performance gain, not a mobility measurement. The wording overreaches from correlation to a causal mechanism. The useful refinement is a proposed mechanism with the mobility endpoint and the SEM/CTEM observations as evidence, linked under the carrier-transport aspect. No observation is removed, and the performance claim n01 remains intact.
</think>

The authors attribute this mainly to silicon absorption combined with MWCNT properties, but silicon alone can produce photocurrent under zero bias. The MWCNT interlayer is conductive, so it is not isolated from the Al top contact, and the spectral series uses band-pass filters that pass the entire band. The same data also show that the 700 °C treatment reduced tensile strength to 298 MPa (o35), and that HD CFRP at 700 °C retained higher strength (o37). So the gain is linked to the treatment, not to the Ni coating alone. The interfacial observations (o17, o18) show the Ni/AC two-phase interface becoming more continuous and less strained after LH to 700 °C, which is consistent with the claim but does not show that the Ni-derived structures caused the gain. The pristine CFRP and uncoated CFRP heat-treated at high temperature also gained ductility (o33, o34), which shows that the effect can occur without Ni coating. So the claim needs to be narrowed to the LD CFRP 700 °C comparison. The other tensile claims (n03) and the interfacial claim (n07) stay as they are because they are not what the claim asserts.

<think>
n15 says high-resistance coatings make the impedance contrast between intact and breached zones large, so a small bare patch produces a large noise current relative to the intact surface. The simulation has no real measured ZRA signal, so the authors' explanation is a computational mechanism. The visible predictions that could support it are o09 (2-4% detectable at Rf,sp > 1000 ohm cm2, 0.05 cm2) and o12 (2% at A = 1.0 cm2, Rf,sp = 1200 ohm cm2). Both depend on the coating resistance in the same way as n15 predicts, but they are also the predictions of the two-zone model that b05 and b06 already use to calculate the threshold. A low-resistance coating (o10: ~25% at Rf,sp = 100 ohm cm2) behaves the other way, as expected from the model. The alternative I add is therefore the two-zone model itself: the coating resistance sets the noise current of the bare zone relative to the intact zone, and the threshold depends on that ratio. It is not a competing explanation for the same data. The only way to distinguish the two is to vary the coating resistance while keeping the coating's effect on the impedance model unchanged, for example by changing the Rf,sp of the intact zone only, or by measuring the coating's actual EIS and using it in the simulation. That is a verification need, not a map change.
</think>

The formulations reduced infarct size (o03, o04, o05), TNF-alpha and IL-6 (o13, o14, o15) and MDA and raised SOD and GSH (o16, o17, o18, o19). The combination effects are not greater than the high-dose effects in the preventive model (o03) and are greater than the high-dose effects in the treatment model (o04). The mechanistic claim is that the formulations work through inhibited inflammation and oxidative stress. The alternative is that the formulations reduce infarct size by reducing the amount of injured tissue. The alternative shares the infarct-size endpoint with the mechanism; the two can be distinguished by comparing the formulations with a comparable non-antioxidant, non-anti-inflammatory formulation and by measuring infarct size when inflammation and oxidative stress are raised by a separate intervention. The visible data do not establish that the alternative is the correct explanation, and the mechanism is not refuted by the alternative.

The refinement replaces the exclusive attribution with a candidate attribution and keeps the evidence and relationships intact.

That observation would show whether the loss is a property of the LW-CKFH sample or of the exposure.

limitations: Red rust is taken by the authors as base-metal oxidation (bg10); the authors do not report the inspection interval.

No change to n10 is required; the unresolved questions are the endpoint definition and field exposure.

<think>
The current mechanism says red-rust time depends on total zinc thickness. The visible evidence does not measure zinc consumption, so the alternative that Teflon wiping leaves the intermetallic sublayer thicker and more protective is testable. A Teflon coating with a thicker sublayer would oxidize faster, so the red-rust times of the Teflon samples would fall. A wax coating with a thinner sublayer would oxidize slower, so its red-rust times would rise. The wax samples already have the higher red-rust times, so this prediction is falsified. The alternative survives only if the Teflon coatings oxidize slower than expected for their thinner total zinc. That is a possible, unverified explanation, but not the only one. The main result is that Teflon-wiped coatings give a consistent red-rust time of 120 h, while wax-wiped coatings give 168-264 h, and the thinner Teflon coatings have a thicker sublayer.
</think>

add_nodes.statement: For a given electrode area A and sampling rate f, the corrosion noise RMS Icorr,bare (bare zone) and Icorr,coated (coated zone) scale with A, as do the ECG-induced current and the instrumental floor (amplifier noise + ADC step).
The ECG-induced current is the product of the ECG voltage and the loop impedance Zloop(Rs, Ze, Rshunt) for the electrode area and sampling rate.
The instrumental floor is the amplifier noise RMS plus the ADC step, both of which scale with the sampling rate f.

For a given electrode area A and sampling rate f, the minimum detectable breach fraction theta_det(N) is the smallest breach fraction that can be reliably distinguished from the intact state over N independent recordings.
theta_det(N) depends on the electrode area A, sampling rate f and number of recordings N, with smaller theta_det(N) for larger A, larger f and larger N.

The four candidate metrics (full RMS current, 1 s moving-average RMS, residual RMS, Chebyshev coefficients) extract different amounts of information from the same composite signal, and the most informative metric depends on the signal-to-noise ratio and the sampling rate.

findings.description: The objective combines three separate questions: coating thickness, coating quality and corrosion resistance, which should be addressed by distinct aspects.
Thickness is measured by gravimetric mt and calculated t, validated by SEM tv and EDX composition.
Coating quality combines microhardness, SEM morphology and interfacial sublayer.
EDX mapping is a distinct compositional endpoint.
Microhardness is a distinct mechanical endpoint.
Corrosion resistance is a distinct endpoint from thickness and quality.
No EDX thickness profile is visible in the packet.
The SEM tv dispersion and pad clamping pressure are not reported.
No field or electrochemical corrosion measurement is part of the study.

o01 shows no oxygen-release difference between HPC@Gel and HB-PDA@Gel in deoxygenated saline. The hemoglobin is only a fraction of the hydrogel by mass (o03); the nanoparticles' hydrodynamic diameter is 38 nm (o03), and the hydrogel is a 3D network (e01). So the extra 10-15% oxygen in HB-PDA@Gel (o01) is small relative to the volume of the 100-µL implant. That makes an oxygen-delivery explanation weak. The alternative stays within the study: the CCQD fraction in HB-PDA@Gel (15% by mass) contains more iron, which is a heme-like metal, than HPC@Gel (5% by mass). The two groups differ in composition, and in the radical-scavenging assay (o02) the HB-containing formulation has higher DPPH and H2O2 scavenging than the CCQDs@Gel group (i08). So the difference in HIF-1α+ neurons could come from iron-dependent changes in the tissue. I add it as a competing candidate, link it to n36, and mark the visible evidence. The test is a matched oxygen-delivery comparison, for example with a non-hemoglobin iron source.
</think>

<think>
The existing nerve-account explanation is that circulating MG53 improves nerve preservation through STAT6-dependent macrophage polarization. The observations supporting it are the genotype comparisons and the STAT6 inhibition. But the map also contains a separate systemic delivery aspect with its own observations. The delivery arm raises MG53 in serum and cornea, with injury area, vascularization and opacity reduced and nerve area increased at day 10. Those are the same readouts that the genotype comparisons use, and the delivery arm's MG53 increase precedes the injury. A reasonable alternative is that the delivery arm works partly through an off-target effect of the modRNA on the cornea, because the delivery route is intramuscular, the modRNA is injected at days -2, 0 and 2, and the cornea is measured at day 10. The existing observations do not separate that route from the MG53 route, so the alternative is proposed as a competing explanation rather than as a finding that the current explanation is wrong.
</think>

findings.description: The LDH release and trypan blue exclusion assays are two measures of the same endpoint, viability, in the same donor cells, at the same time, using the same untreated control comparator. The source reports them together as one pooled viability panel, and the LDH readout is defined in the Methods as a cytotoxicity percentage relative to spontaneous release and maximal lysis, so it measures a different quantity from the percentage of trypan-blue-excluding cells. The pair duplicates the same purpose and should become one plan.

The Seahorse glycoPER and lactate assay measure different endpoints: proton efflux over minutes and the accumulated secreted product in 24-h conditioned medium. They use the same cultures and the same stimulation, but they are not duplicates of one another.

The conditioned-medium transfer and the Transwell co-culture both measure the recipient response to donor-derived factors, but one is a single transfer with a 24-h exposure and the other is a continuous 24-h non-contact exchange. They are two separate tests of the same pathway and should not be merged.

proposed_updates.rationale: The two assays are two measures of the same endpoint, viability, in the same donor cells, at the same time, using the same untreated control comparator. The LDH readout is defined in the Methods as a cytotoxicity percentage relative to spontaneous release and maximal lysis, so it measures a different quantity from the percentage of trypan-blue-excluding cells. The pair duplicates the same purpose and should become one plan; the LDH assay's own readout is retained as a separate observation under the consolidated plan.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Partly supported: the EV-depleted plasma experiments show that the senescence-inducing activity is not carried by extracellular vesicles, and TGFβ2 is elevated in heart failure plasma and TAC mice. These observations are not sufficient to show that TGFβ2 is the senescence-inducing factor or that it acts in free soluble form in endothelial cells.
limitations: No experiment isolated TGFβ2 from plasma
No measurement of TGFβ2 activity or receptor signaling in the endothelial cells
aspect_assessments.rationale: The EV-depletion result addresses the form of the factor, and the TGFβ2 measurements address its elevation, but neither tests sufficiency.
aspect_assessments.scope: Endothelial cells exposed to dialyzed plasma or its EV-depleted supernatant, with TGFβ2 measured in dialyzed plasma and mouse plasma

aspect_assessments.assessment: Supported at the observed scope: plasma from heart failure patients and from TAC mice induces SA-β-gal in cultured endothelial cells, and TGFβ2 is elevated in both plasma types.
limitations: SA-β-gal is an indirect senescence marker
aspect_assessments.rationale: The two endpoints agree and the EV-depletion result is consistent with the free soluble form claim.
aspect_assessments.scope: Cultured endothelial cells, dialyzed plasma and EV-depleted plasma supernatant

findings.description: n11 states TGFβ2 as the senescence-inducing factor and asserts that it is predominantly free soluble, but none of the linked observations isolates TGFβ2 from plasma. The EV-depleted plasma experiments show that the activity persists after vesicle removal, which is consistent with a free soluble factor but does not identify it.
The EV-depleted plasma experiments are consistent with TGFβ2 acting in free soluble form, but they do not show that TGFβ2 is the factor responsible for the senescence induction.

information_requests: Whether TGFβ2 receptor signaling or downstream readouts were measured in endothelial cells exposed to dialyzed plasma or EV-depleted plasma.

replace_nodes.statement: After extracellular-vesicle removal, the senescence-inducing activity of heart failure plasma persists in the depleted supernatant, and TGFβ2 is elevated in heart failure plasma and in TAC mouse plasma. This is consistent with TGFβ2 acting as a free soluble factor, but the visible experiments do not isolate TGFβ2 from plasma or show that it is the senescence-inducing factor in endothelial cells.

proposed_updates.rationale: The revised wording keeps the evidence the observations support and removes the part that the observations cannot support: sufficiency of TGFβ2 as the senescence-inducing factor and its exclusive free soluble form in endothelial cells.

verification_needs.comparison_or_control: EV-depleted heart failure plasma versus EV-depleted heart failure plasma lacking TGFβ2
missing_design_information: Concentration of dialyzed plasma used in the EV-depletion experiments
needed_observations: SA-β-gal expression in endothelial cells after dialyzed heart failure plasma is depleted of TGFβ2
TGFβ2 receptor activation and downstream signaling in endothelial cells exposed to dialyzed heart failure plasma
verification_needs.unresolved_question: Is TGFβ2 the factor responsible for the senescence-induction effect of heart failure plasma?
verification_needs.why_informative: Depletion of TGFβ2 from plasma would separate the factor from other plasma components, while receptor signaling would test whether the factor acts through its known pathway.

add_nodes.statement: Fe substitution produces a sulfur-vacancy-rich Fe-WS2 with altered electronic structure, GOx loading, and NIR-to-heat conversion.
The nanozyme has enzyme-like catalytic activities (POD-, GOx-, CAT- and GPx-like) in cell-free buffer assays.
The material kills planktonic MRSA and E. coli and their biofilms, with and without NIR irradiation.
Bacterial killing involves ROS generation, lipid peroxidation, GSH/GSSG redox imbalance, GPX4 inactivation, ETC and energy metabolism impairment, and apoptosis.
The material is compatible with fibroblasts, erythrocytes and LPS-stimulated macrophages in vitro.
The material induces M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization in vitro.
It accelerates healing of MRSA-infected diabetic wounds.
ROS generation is increased in bacteria exposed to the material with or without NIR.
Lipid peroxidation and MDA are increased in bacteria exposed to the material with or without NIR.
GSH/GSSG ratio and GSH-Px activity are changed in bacteria exposed to the material with or without NIR.
GPX4 is inactivated in bacteria exposed to the material with or without NIR.
ETC function and ATP production are impaired in bacteria exposed to the material with or without NIR.
Apoptosis is induced in bacteria exposed to the material with or without NIR.
Respiratory complexes I-III are impaired in bacteria exposed to the material with or without NIR.
ROS generation is increased in E. coli after RNA sequencing, and its ferroptosis-related expression is changed.
Bacterial clearance, wound repair and inflammation are improved in MRSA-infected diabetic wounds.
Bacterial clearance is improved in the infected wound.
Wound repair is accelerated.
Inflammation is reduced in the infected wound.

The current map explains the eradication result as a consequence of biofilm architecture (n08). The observations show that AgNPs and LEO inhibit growth and biofilm formation at low concentrations. The same concentrations applied to pre-formed biofilms produced no significant difference from the positive control. The alternative is that the AgNPs and LEO in the eradication wells have less bioavailability than in the formation wells. In the formation wells, the agents are present from inoculation, so the biofilm forms in contact with them. In the eradication wells, the biofilm is formed first, then the agents are added. The biofilm matrix might bind and retain the agents, reducing their local concentration. The visible observations do not measure agent concentration in the wells, so this is a candidate explanation. It does not contradict the current explanation, because both would predict no significant reduction. A test would be to measure the agent concentration in wells with and without pre-formed biofilm and to measure biofilm biomass with a method that does not rely on stain release. The two explanations are not mutually exclusive, so the alternative should be added to the map rather than replacing n08.
</think>

The correct refinement is therefore to reword n08 to the system in which the measurement was made and to keep the system-specific part of the mechanism statement, since the packet does not state which system produced the rescue. The other claims stay as they are.

The refinement keeps the engulfment comparison as a separate comparison, the structural prediction as a computational model, and the downstream readouts as measurements of the signalling cascade that the structural account is meant to explain. aspect_assessments.assessment: The claim is not supported as it stands. The visible engulfment comparison shows comparable oAβ-pHrodo uptake by V2 AXL-CAR-BV2 cells relative to V1 AXL-CAR-BV2 cells (o04), whereas the downstream comparison shows Socs1 and Socs3 upregulated in V2 cells but not in V1 cells (o03) and higher phospho-STAT1 in V2 cells than in V1 cells at 60 min (o05). The structural account asserts that the phagocytic difference has a structural basis, but the two readouts do not move together, so the structural explanation for the downstream difference is not yet tested.
limitations: The engulfment comparison was made in BV2 cells, and the downstream readouts in RAW264.7 cells.
No measurement of downstream signalling was made in V1 AXL-CAR cells in the same experiment as the engulfment measurement.
The structural prediction is an in silico model.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The claim attributes the downstream difference to a structural difference that is not reflected in the engulfment readout. The refinement separates that attribution from the two measured comparisons.
aspect_assessments.scope: Mouse RAW264.7 and BV2 cells under oAβ stimulation; BV2 engulfment comparison only.

aspect_assessments.assessment: The two-V1-versus-V2 AXL-CAR comparisons are supported. o03 shows Socs1 and Socs3 upregulated in V2 cells but not in V1 cells, and o05 shows higher phospho-STAT1 in V2 cells than in V1 cells at 60 min.
limitations: The phospho-STAT1 result is reported at one time point, with a comparator group that is not explicitly identified in the quantification legend.
The engulfment comparison was made in BV2 cells, and the downstream readouts in RAW264.7 cells.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The two readouts move in the direction the structural account attributes to the structural difference.
aspect_assessments.scope: RAW264.7 cells for the downstream readouts; BV2 cells for the engulfment readout.

aspect_assessments.assessment: The anti-inflammatory phenotype of the TAM-CAR design is supported across the three inflammatory paradigms: AXL-CAR reduced Il1a, Il1b and Tnf relative to the truncated-CAR control under acute co-stimulation, and attenuated the primed response with the strongest suppression of Il1a and Il1b and second strongest suppression of Tnf; AXL-CAR-BV2 cells kept Il1a, Il1b and Il6 low relative to EGFP control cells under oAβ alone.
limitations: The priming model uses a different time course and dosing than the acute model, and the oAβ-only comparison is limited to three cytokines.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The phenotype is assessed across three different conditions and cell lines.
aspect_assessments.scope: Mouse RAW264.7 and BV2 cells; three inflammatory paradigms.

findings.description: The structural account of the V1/V2 AXL-CAR comparison is not testable from the visible evidence: it asserts that the phagocytic difference has a structural basis, but the engulfment comparison shows comparable uptake while the downstream comparison shows stronger downstream signalling in V2 cells. The structural prediction (o06) is a model of the dimer interface and does not establish the causal link between interfacial stability and downstream signalling.

The downstream readouts move in the direction the structural account attributes to the structural difference, but the engulfment comparison was made in BV2 cells and the downstream readouts in RAW264.7 cells, so the two readouts cannot be read as one experiment.

information_requests: The identity of the comparator group used for the phospho-STAT1 quantification (Truncated versus V2-AXL-CAR versus V1 AXL-CAR) and the number of independent replicate fields.

replace_nodes.statement: The stronger downstream TAM signalling and induction of anti-inflammatory regulators in V2 AXL-CAR cells relative to V1 AXL-CAR cells are explained by the enhanced interfacial stability of the V2 CAR design. The structural prediction of multiple interfacial hydrogen bonds in the V2 dimer is consistent with this account but does not establish it; it does not explain the comparable oAβ-pHrodo uptake by V2 AXL-CAR-BV2 cells relative to V1 AXL-CAR-BV2 cells (o04).

proposed_updates.rationale: The refinement keeps the engulfment comparison as a separate comparison, the structural prediction as a computational model, and the downstream readouts as measurements of the signalling cascade that the structural account is meant to explain. It also leaves the direction of the comparison explicit: the structural account explains the stronger downstream response of V2 cells relative to V1 cells, not the opposite. No observation is removed or relinked, and the claim is not made stronger.

<think>
The visible comparison that separates the two claims is the donor cell population. The AXL-CAR-iMGL group also received hCSF1 expression, which the authors later cite as an independent survival advantage for transplanted cells (o16). The EGFP-iMGL group received no such transduction. Because engrafted iMGLs are defined as human CD45-positive, CD11b-positive cells within the total microglial gate (c04), the difference in plaque burden could reflect a larger number of transplanted cells in the AXL-CAR group. The visible records support that difference: the AXL-CAR group had about 10-15% of hippocampal microglia from the transplanted population at 7 and 14 days (o17), while the EGFP-iMGL group had about the same proportion (o17). The cell number is therefore not directly visible here. A candidate that can be tested is that AXL-CAR-iMGLs survive better than EGFP-iMGLs in the recipient's brain, reach a larger donor-derived population in the hippocampus, and then each cell clears Aβ at its own rate, so that the lower plaque area in the AXL-CAR group comes from more transplanted cells rather than from higher clearance per cell. The competing claim, that the CAR increases per-cell clearance, is already supported by the plaque-area comparison (o18) and by the colocalization observation (o24), so the candidate must be stated as a possible alternative, not as a conclusion. The test is a cell-specific Aβ quantification, for example total Aβ area divided by the number of donor-derived cells, in both groups. It should also use the same sections and ROI as the plaque-area measurement, because the plaque-area comparison already counts all plaques and does not distinguish donor from host origin (c04). The existing plaque-area and plaque-number comparisons are retained as evidence for the measured burden, and the histological observations for neuronal and synaptic endpoints remain unchanged. A candidate for the cell number is not required for the distinction between the two claims.
</think>

The claim's wording that the lower burden is explained by CAR-mediated per-cell clearance is not tested here; the visible records do not show whether the transplanted cell population differs in size or survival between the two groups.
limitations: No cell-specific Aβ quantification is visible; plaque area counts all plaques in the ROI.
The donor cell population size is not directly visible for the two cell groups.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Neuronal layer thickness in CA1 was significantly higher in AXL-CAR-iMGL-treated mice than in PBS-treated mice, and synaptophysin density did not differ across the compared groups.
limitations: No synaptic-loss measurement is visible.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The visible observations directly address this aspect.
aspect_assessments.scope: Hippocampal CA1 and dentate gyrus at three weeks.

findings.description: The AXL-CAR-iMGL group received lentiviral transduction with hCSF1 expression, which the authors later cite as an independent survival advantage for transplanted cells (o16). Because engrafted iMGLs are defined as human CD45-positive, CD11b-positive cells within the total microglial gate (c04), the difference in plaque burden could reflect a larger number of transplanted cells in the AXL-CAR group.

The plaque-area comparison (o18) and the colocalization observation (o24) are consistent with a CAR-conferred increase in per-cell Aβ clearance, so that remains the competing account rather than the candidate itself.

add_nodes.statement: Candidate alternative: the lower hippocampal Aβ-positive area in AXL-CAR-iMGL-treated mice relative to EGFP-iMGL-treated mice at three weeks is explained by a larger number of transplanted AXL-CAR-iMGLs in the hippocampus, which reach the ROI in larger numbers or survive longer in the recipient's brain, rather than by an increased per-cell Aβ clearance rate.

proposed_updates.rationale: The visible comparison that separates the two claims is the donor cell population. The AXL-CAR-iMGL group also received hCSF1 expression, which the authors later cite as an independent survival advantage for transplanted cells (o16). Because engrafted iMGLs are defined as human CD45-positive, CD11b-positive cells within the total microglial gate (c04), the difference in plaque burden could reflect a larger number of transplanted cells in the AXL-CAR group. The competing claim that the CAR increases per-cell clearance is already supported by the plaque-area comparison (o18) and by the colocalization observation (o24), so the candidate must be stated as a possible alternative, not as a conclusion. The test is a cell-specific Aβ quantification, for example total Aβ area divided by the number of donor-derived cells, in both groups.

add_nodes.statement: Proposed alternative: the 2-DG-sensitive rise in glycoPER also carries a 2-DG-insensitive metabolic change that contributes to cytokine output, such as a rise in the citrate/malate ratio or the NAD+/NADH ratio, and the cytokine difference reflects that metabolic change rather than the flux difference.

<think>
The proposed mechanism links response/recovery time to the viscoelastic rebound of the sponge and film. The test at e07 changed pressure by moving the motorized stage, so the sponge and film were compressed more deeply at higher pressure. The observed times increased from 350/340 to 540/550 ms. That is consistent with the mechanism, but it is also consistent with a different explanation. The hold protocol at e08, which held the pressure for 4 s, showed no drift at 5.5-15 kPa, which is not what the proposed mechanism predicts. If the hold phase were removed, the sensor would relax during the hold, and the resistance would fall toward the unloaded value. At the same time, the response time is the time from the start of loading to the peak of the response, and the recovery time is the time from the start of unloading to the return to the initial resistance. The visible protocol has loading and unloading each lasting 1 s and a 4 s hold. That means the recovery time includes a 4 s hold during which the sensor is at constant pressure and the resistance is not changing. If the hold phase were removed, the recovery time would be measured from the start of unloading to the return to the initial resistance. The hold phase therefore changes the recovery time even though it does not change the applied pressure. The two explanations predict different outcomes in that protocol. The proposed alternative is therefore a competing explanation that can be tested by repeating the hold protocol without the hold phase and measuring the response and recovery times, then comparing them with the hold protocol. It does not replace the recorded explanation, which is supported by its own test.
</think>

findings.description: The existing map and observations cover a single cisplatin AKI model and the DPEP1 mechanism that explains it; they do not cover chemotherapy in tumour-bearing hosts on the same schedule.

add_nodes.statement: CTT/MPDA@L-Ser nanoparticles reduce cisplatin-induced kidney injury in tumour-bearing hosts receiving cisplatin chemotherapy on the same schedule as in the cisplatin AKI model: 30 min before cisplatin and on days 1 and 2, with all animals sacrificed 72 h after model establishment.
In tumour-bearing cisplatin AKI mice, drug-loaded CTT/MPDA@L-Ser nanoparticles accumulate in kidneys relative to drug-free CTT/MPDA and to healthy mice.
In tumour-bearing cisplatin AKI mice, treatment with CTT/MPDA@L-Ser reduces kidney injury markers, renal function and systemic toxicity relative to free cilastatin and to the cisplatin-only model.
In tumour-bearing cisplatin AKI mice, the effect of CTT/MPDA@L-Ser on kidney injury is mediated by cilastatin release, DPEP1 inhibition and GPX4/SLC7A11 restoration.

proposed_updates.rationale: The scope extension calls for a new condition, so I add an aspect for it with sub-aspects that cover the new exposure, the new tumour-bearing kidney and the unchanged mechanism. <think>
The first set of observations supports endothelial senescence. o12 and o13 come from different species and model systems: o12 is staining of SA-β-gal in retinal endothelium of TAC versus sham mice, and o13 is SA-β-gal staining in human endothelial cells exposed to heart failure patient plasma. o14 is the same system as o13 but with mouse plasma from TAC versus sham donors. o49 adds a transcriptomic readout of inflammatory and senescence-related pathways in endothelial cells exposed to mouse plasma. These are all indirect senescence markers, not cell-cycle or secretory measurements. The second set shows that endothelial senescence tracks with microglial activation. o36 is morphology in vivo, o37 is an animal-level correlation, and o38 is primary microglia exposed to conditioned medium from endothelial cells. The third set shows that microglial depletion improves function and structure in TAC mice. o41 and o42 are the retinal readouts, and o39 and o40 are the microglial readouts from the same conditioned medium. The microglial readouts are in culture, so they are not a direct readout of retinal microglia. The strongest remaining link is the conditional depletion, which changes the mouse's microglia and restores the retinal readouts, and the microglial activation readouts, which are in the same animals as the endothelial senescence readouts. The design does not test whether endothelial senescence precedes microglial activation, so a prospective manipulation of endothelial senescence followed by a measurement of microglial activation would separate cause from association. The most direct way to do that is to condition endothelial cells from TAC mice with dialyzed plasma or with recombinant TGFβ2 and compare microglial activation with endothelial senescence. The microglia should be from the same retinas as the endothelial cells, so the cultures are not the only possible source. A second manipulation is to deplete microglia and see whether endothelial senescence persists; that would test whether microglia are required for the senescence. A third is to measure the plasma factor directly, for example by measuring TGFβ2 in plasma or by blocking it and measuring endothelial senescence and retinal damage. The three manipulations are complementary and should be carried out together.
</think>

aspect_assessments.assessment: The visible evidence supports both accounts equally well. In mice, Dclk1 deletion lowers DCLK1, phospho-DCLK1 and fibrotic markers and lowers phospho-Akt and phospho-Smad3. In cultured cells, DCLK1 knockdown lowers fibronectin and CTGF, and Smad3 binds the CTGF promoter. Because the coimmunoprecipitation and ChIP experiments are reported without an unstimulated or IgG comparison arm, they cannot by themselves show direct DCLK1-Smad3 binding.
limitations: Coimmunoprecipitation and ChIP readouts do not distinguish direct DCLK1-Smad3 binding from an association mediated by a shared downstream signal.
No unstimulated or IgG comparison arm is stated for the coimmunoprecipitation or ChIP assays.
The mouse phospho-Akt reduction is equally consistent with less injury or with feedback in fibrotic tissue.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The two accounts make the same predictions for all visible readouts, and the only distinguishing test is the order of Akt and DCLK1.
aspect_assessments.scope: Mouse BLM cohort at day 21 and cultured NHLFs stimulated with TGF-β.

findings.description: The coimmunoprecipitation and ChIP readouts do not by themselves establish direct DCLK1-Smad3 binding, and the mouse phospho-Akt reduction is not a test of the ordering of Akt relative to DCLK1.

information_requests: Whether the coimmunoprecipitation and ChIP assays included an unstimulated or IgG comparison arm.

add_nodes.statement: Candidate alternative: DCLK1 associates with Smad3 through a shared downstream signal such as Akt, and the lower phospho-Akt and phospho-Smad3 in Dclk1-deleted mice and the lower fibronectin and CTGF after DCLK1 knockdown reflect a loss of that downstream signal rather than a direct DCLK1-Smad3 interaction. This account predicts that the fibrotic effects of DCLK1 knockdown persist with a kinase-dead DCLK1 mutant that binds Smad3 but cannot phosphorylate it, whereas the upstream account predicts they do not.

proposed_updates.rationale: The visible evidence is equally consistent with both accounts, so the alternative is written as a candidate explanation linked to the coimmunoprecipitation and ChIP nodes. It is distinguished from the present interpretation by a test of the order of Akt and DCLK1.

needed_observations: Coimmunoprecipitation of DCLK1 and Smad3 from unstimulated NHLFs, with the same antibody and bead protocol

verification_needs.why_informative: Direct DCLK1-Smad3 binding is detected in TGF-β-stimulated cells only if it persists in unstimulated cells. The IgG arm establishes that the enrichment in the stimulated condition is specific to DCLK1.

verification_needs.why_informative: If the fibrotic effects persist with a kinase-dead DCLK1 mutant, the alternative is favoured; if they are lost, the upstream account is favoured.

<think>
The current account attributes the U46619 hypercontractility and the oxidative markers to NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species. o11 shows that apocynin at 300 micromol/L normalises the response of 40 ppm rings to the level of non-incubated controls, yet o12 leaves the 80 ppm Emax unchanged after apocynin. The same preparation also shows a marked drop in glutathione peroxidase activity at 80 ppm (o15). Apocynin is an NADPH oxidase inhibitor with direct antioxidant activity (k03), so a fall in glutathione peroxidase could leave reactive oxygen species unchecked, and the apocynin arm could thus hide rather than establish NADPH oxidase involvement. The alternative is therefore that the lower glutathione peroxidase at 80 ppm allows reactive oxygen species to rise more freely, making the rings less sensitive to apocynin inhibition. It predicts that the 80 ppm Emax would fall after apocynin, which the data do not show, and that the apocynin effect would be smaller at 80 ppm than at 40 ppm. A matched incubation across all groups, with and without N-acetylcysteine, would separate these accounts.
</think>

add_nodes.statement: Proposed treatment target: inhibit the TXA2 pathway in rats made hypertensive by chronic CdCl2 exposure, and assess whether such inhibition lowers systolic blood pressure.

Proposed mechanism: TXA2 receptor activation contributes to the CdCl2-induced increase in U46619 contraction, and TXA2 receptor antagonism reduces the vascular response and lowers blood pressure through that pathway.

The map's mechanism requires SnO2 diffusion into the secondary particle and localized reaction at grain boundaries. That is inferred from the 700 °C intermediate, whose HRTEM shows SnO2 lattice fringes at grain boundaries and a lower surface Sn/Ni ratio than the final product, and from the DFT prediction that NCA + SnO2 releases O2 at 1.51 eV. The visible evidence also shows that the coating changes the product: PC-NCA90 is agglomerated, SC-Sn-NCA90 is single-crystalline and dispersed, and the transformation is complete at 0.8 mol% Sn and 24 h at 750 °C. These observations are consistent with the current mechanism. They are also compatible with a different route: the coating may reduce the viscosity of the precursor slurry, allowing the particles to remain separated during heating and preventing secondary-particle agglomeration, so that the normal phase evolution at 750 °C yields single crystals without grain-boundary elimination. The two routes differ in what they predict for the final product: the current mechanism predicts Li2SnO3 and a surface Sn layer, while the slurry route predicts no Sn in the final product. A comparison of the final products of the two routes, plus a direct measurement of Sn in the final product of the coated precursor, would distinguish them.
</think>

These aspects are ordered so that the barrier aspects depend on the Ni-P layer aspects. No visible observations are supplied, so every aspect is stated as a verification need.

findings.description: The objective combines a Ni-P layer on a TE element and Cu diffusion across it; the validation requirements q01-q04 must be organized into aspects for each system.

add_nodes.statement: Electroless Ni-P plating on polymer-coated cylindrical p-type Bi2-xSbxTe3 TE elements, with SDS added to the bath and selective deposition on the exposed top and bottom faces.
Selective deposition of the Ni-P layer on the exposed TE element surfaces, with no deposition on the polymer-coated side surfaces of the elements.
Uniformity and defect minimization of the Ni-P layer on the exposed TE element surface.
Barrier performance of the Ni-P layer against Cu diffusion into the TE element during heat treatment.
Formation of Cu intermetallic compounds between the Cu layer and the Ni-P layer on the TE element after heat treatment.

proposed_updates.rationale: The four aspects represent the four validation requirements: selectivity (p01), uniformity (p02), barrier performance (p03) and intermetallic formation (p04). The barrier aspects depend on the Ni-P layer aspects, so p03 and p04 are linked to p02, and p02 is linked to p00. Selectivity must be tested on the polymer-coated region, which cannot be plated.

verification_needs.comparison_or_control: SDS-free vs SDS-containing Ni-P layer on TE elements, with and without Cu electroplating and heat treatment.
needed_observations: Selective Ni-P deposition on exposed TE element faces and absence of Ni-P on polymer-coated side surfaces, confirmed by element mapping.
verification_needs.unresolved_question: Does the Ni-P layer form only on the exposed TE element surfaces?
verification_needs.why_informative: A selective layer is required before the barrier aspects can be tested.

verification_needs.comparison_or_control: Ni-P layer with and without Cu electroplating, and without and with heat treatment.
needed_observations: Thickness, roughness, surface composition and defect density of the Ni-P layer on the exposed TE element surface.
verification_needs.unresolved_question: Is the Ni-P layer uniform and defect-minimized on the TE element surface?
verification_needs.why_informative: A uniform, defect-free layer is required before barrier performance can be assessed.

verification_needs.comparison_or_control: Cu/Ni-P/TE elements heat-treated at 100 °C vs 200 °C, with and without the Ni-P layer.
needed_observations: Cu concentration in the TE element as a function of time, with a control without the Ni-P layer.
verification_needs.unresolved_question: Does the Ni-P layer suppress Cu diffusion into the TE element?
verification_needs.why_informative: A diffusion measurement directly tests barrier performance.

verification_needs.comparison_or_control: Cu/Ni-P/TE elements with and without the Ni-P layer, and with and without heat treatment.
needed_observations: Phase composition of the Cu/Ni-P/TE element interface and intermetallic compound thickness after heat treatment.
verification_needs.unresolved_question: Do Cu intermetallic compounds form between the Cu layer and the TE element?
verification_needs.why_informative: Intermetallic formation is a direct phase readout of diffusion.

These require separate comparisons. Formation is a coating-only property (TP vs TPB vs TPBE), release is a time-resolved TPBE+NIR vs TPBE comparison, cell responses are TPBE+NIR vs TPBE, TP vs TPB vs TPBE, and TPBE+NIR vs T, neurovascularization is TPBE+NIR vs TPBE, and safety is TPBE+NIR vs T. Each comparison needs a readout that distinguishes the class, such as spectroscopy for release and neurovascular markers for the in vivo network. Safety is a separate aspect because it does not directly test regeneration.

The map already names the selectivity, surface/interfacial state and barrier-performance components of the SDS effect. The aspect wording is broad, and the evidence includes contact-angle, SEM and XPS comparisons between Bath A and Bath B, and EPMA and line-scan comparisons of the Cu/Ni-P/TE cross-section. The question is whether the map needs more explicit sub-aspects. The selectivity component already has the contact-angle and OM series; the surface and interfacial state component already has the XPS series; and the barrier-performance component already has the heat-treatment series. The contact-angle series covers both substrates and shows the TE element is wettable by Bath B and the polymer is not, so the plating selectivity aspect is not redundant with it. The EPMA and line-scan series show no Cu diffusion beyond the Ni-P layer at both temperatures, so the barrier aspect is not redundant with it either. The current map therefore has the right number of components, and the appropriate next step is to assess the evidence and check whether any component is supported at a different scope than stated. I do not add a sub-aspect for that.
</think>

findings.description: The selectivity component is already represented by the contact-angle and cross-sectional OM series, and the contact-angle series shows that the TE element is wettable by Bath B and the polymer is not, which directly addresses selectivity.
The surface and interfacial state component is already represented by the XPS series, which compares Bath A and Bath B on the outermost surface and reports Ni 2p, S 2p and P 2p spectra.

The barrier-performance component is already represented by the EPMA and line-scan series of the Cu/Ni-P/TE cross-section, and the heat-treatment observations show no Cu diffusion beyond the Ni-P layer.

The SDS concentration series shows that the extent of Ni-P coverage on the TE element surface and plating selectivity relative to the polymer region depend on SDS concentration, with an intermediate concentration required for both, so the selectivity aspect also carries a concentration-dependent sub-component that is supported by the OM series.

parsed_answer.no_change_reason: The aspect n15 already contains the selectivity, surface/interfacial state and barrier-performance components of the SDS effect, and each component is represented by a relevant observation series: the contact-angle and cross-sectional OM series for selectivity, the XPS series for surface and interfacial states, and the EPMA and line-scan series for barrier performance. The contact-angle series covers both substrates and shows that the TE element is wettable by Bath B and the polymer is not, so the selectivity aspect is not redundant with it; the EPMA and line-scan series show no Cu diffusion beyond the Ni-P layer at both temperatures, so the barrier aspect is not redundant with it either. The current map therefore has the right number of components, and the appropriate next step is to assess the evidence and check whether any component is supported at a different scope than stated. I do not add a sub-aspect for that.

The visible selectivity observations support a wetting-contrast mechanism: the TE element has low contact angle (9°) and the polymer has high contact angle (56°), so the bath wets the TE element and not the polymer, and SDS lowers the contact angle further. But the SDS series shows that without SDS, the Ni-P layer is thin and discontinuous (o05); with SDS, it is continuous at 0.5 g/L (o07) but extends into the polymer region at 1.0 g/L (o08). These are changes in the deposit itself, not in the bath wettability, so they point to a different explanation. A plausible candidate is that SDS changes the deposit's surface energy. SDS lowers the bath surface tension (o02) and adsorbs on the electrode surface during deposition, which lowers the Ni-P surface energy and makes it more attractive to the bath. The lower-energy Ni-P surface then becomes more wettable, so the bath spreads on it and deposits more Ni-P, while the higher-energy polymer stays wettable and deposits less. This would predict that SDS lowers the Ni-P surface energy, and that the same SDS concentration changes the Ni-P/TE element and Ni-P/polymer contact angles. A measurement of these two contact angles, with the polymer surface and the Ni-P surface of each TE element, would distinguish the two explanations.
</think>

The two child aspects are not independent because the bulk Sn is the source of the Li2SnO3, so their relationship is recorded as a proposal. The existing aspect n11 is left intact because it is a comparative claim whose wording is supported by the child aspects.

findings.description: The current mechanism aspect combines two separate effects: structural (H2-H3 peak, Rct, RCEI, DLi+ and cracking) and interfacial (Li2SnO3 phase, TOF-SIMS and CEI interpretation). The authors' interpretations (i03-i06) are consistent with the evidence but do not identify which effect is responsible for which performance difference. Splitting the aspect keeps the attribution open and records the causal link to bulk doping as a proposal.

add_nodes.statement: The structural component of the dual-site Sn modification: bulk Sn doping reduces the voltage hysteresis and intensity loss of the H2-H3 oxidation peak, lowers the fitted interfacial charge-transfer resistance (Rct) and charge-transfer-inhibiting layer resistance (RCEI), and preserves the apparent Li+ diffusion coefficient (DLi+) during cycling.

The interfacial component of the dual-site Sn modification: a residual surface Li2SnO3 phase of about 8 nm forms a thin, protective CEI that attenuates oxidative decomposition products (LiF2-, PO3-, C2HO-) and suppresses transition-metal dissolution (NiF3-), preventing intergranular cracking.

proposed_updates.rationale: The structural and interfacial effects are measured by different endpoints and have different interpretations (i03-i06), so separating them prevents the two effects from being treated as one undifferentiated explanation. The bulk doping aspect n08 is kept as a proposed explanation of n32 because the Li2SnO3 phase is the residual phase of the coating reaction and the two sites are not independent.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Supported by three linked histological observations in the same cohort at day 21.
limitations: The Methods describe mouse sections as fixed overnight in 4% paraformaldehyde, whereas the fixation record is inconsistent in the source.
aspect_assessments.rationale: All three observations come from the same experiment plan.
aspect_assessments.scope: Day 21 in the genetic cohort.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Supported by four linked observations measuring lung function, microCT, immunoblotting and blood neutrophils in the same cohort at day 21.
limitations: The reported direction of the normalized work of breathing in fibrosis is internally inconsistent in the source.
aspect_assessments.rationale: All four observations come from the same experiment plan.
aspect_assessments.scope: Day 21 in the genetic cohort.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Supported by a fibroblast knockdown comparison and a fibroblast pretreatment comparison.
limitations: The fibroblast pretreatment comparison has no stated vehicle arm.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The two observations use different arms of the same experiment plan.
aspect_assessments.scope: TGF-β-stimulated NHLFs.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Supported by a stimulated-versus-unstimulated occupancy comparison and a DCLK1-versus-IgG occupancy comparison.
limitations: The comparison arm behind the reported enrichment is not stated in the Methods for o14.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The two observations use different arms of the same experiment plan.
aspect_assessments.scope: TGF-β-stimulated fibroblasts.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Supported by three linked observations in the same pharmacological cohort at day 28.
limitations: The Methods state a vehicle arm for control mice; whether the BLM-only comparison group received vehicle is not stated.
aspect_assessments.rationale: All five observations come from the same experiment plan.
aspect_assessments.scope: Day 28 in the pharmacological cohort.

findings.description: e03 and e04 measure the same histological, functional and imaging endpoints in the genetic cohort at day 21, while e17 repeats them in the pharmacological cohort at day 28. e04 adds microCT and blood neutrophils, which e17 repeats.
e06 and e15 test DCLK1 inhibition in fibroblasts with the same readouts, but e15 is the only one that pretreats cells before TGF-β.
e07 and e13 both use ChIP in stimulated fibroblasts, but e07 tests Smad3 and NF-κB p65 occupancy at the DCLK1 promoter while e13 tests DCLK1 occupancy at the CTGF promoter.
e16 and e17 both use the same treatment schedule and the same day 28 endpoint, so they measure the same animal-level endpoints in the same cohort.
e03 and e04 both read H&E and Masson trichrome slides, so they serve the same histology purpose in the genetic cohort.
e04 measures microCT and attenuation histograms in the genetic cohort at day 21, while e17 repeats them in the pharmacological cohort at day 28.
e04 measures blood neutrophils in the genetic cohort at day 21, while e17 repeats it in the pharmacological cohort at day 28.
e03 and e04 measure lung function in the genetic cohort at day 21, while e17 repeats it in the pharmacological cohort at day 28.
e16 and e17 both use the same treatment schedule and the same day 28 endpoint, so they measure the same animal-level endpoints in the same cohort.

proposed_updates.rationale: e03 and e04 measure the same histological, functional and imaging endpoints in the genetic cohort at day 21, while e17 repeats them in the pharmacological cohort at day 28. e04 adds microCT and blood neutrophils, which e17 repeats, so the three plans are not interchangeable. I retain e04 for the microCT and neutrophil measurements and e17 for the pharmacological cohort and day 28 measurements.

aspect_assessments.assessment: The U46619 readout is supported by a higher Emax in rings from animals exposed to 40 ppm and 80 ppm versus CTRL, while pD2 is unchanged. The apocynin arm shows that the response is reduced by apocynin in 80 ppm rings and normalised to CTRL level in 40 ppm rings. The evidence supports a functional response to U46619 and apocynin attenuation of it, without measuring TXA2 receptor number, TXA2 production or downstream signalling.
limitations: No TXA2 receptor, TXA2 production or downstream signalling measurement
No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
The 80 ppm versus 40 ppm comparison lacks a symbol in Table 2 and is stated only in the Results text
aspect_assessments.rationale: o09 and o12 report the U46619 Emax, the between-exposure comparison and the apocynin readouts for both exposure concentrations.
aspect_assessments.scope: Isolated thoracic aortic rings from animals exposed to 40 ppm or 80 ppm CdCl2 for 8 weeks, compared with non-incubated CTRL rings, with apocynin incubation in selected rings.

aspect_assessments.assessment: The claim that TXA2 induces hypercontractility in exposed aortas, that the response is associated with oxidative stress and reversed by apocynin, is supported by the U46619 readout and the apocynin readout. It is not supported as a direct causal link from TXA2 to hypertension.
limitations: Apocynin specificity is not resolved
No TXA2 receptor, TXA2 production or downstream signalling measurement
No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
aspect_assessments.rationale: o09 reports the higher Emax in exposed animals, o11 and o12 report apocynin attenuation of the response in 80 ppm rings and normalisation to CTRL level in 40 ppm rings. Neither measurement tests TXA2 receptor number, TXA2 production or downstream signalling.
aspect_assessments.scope: The U46619 concentration-response readout and the apocynin incubation arm.

aspect_assessments.assessment: The interpretation claim is supported by the apocynin readouts: the response is reduced by apocynin in 80 ppm rings and normalised to CTRL level in 40 ppm rings, so it is not a direct measure of TXA2 signalling or receptor upregulation. The map already contains this interpretation as n12, so the useful change is a refinement edge from n08 to n12 rather than a new aspect.
limitations: Apocynin specificity is not resolved
No direct measurement of reactive oxygen species or nitric oxide
aspect_assessments.rationale: o11 and o12 show that the apocynin arm was run for both exposure concentrations and that the response was reduced by apocynin in 80 ppm rings.
aspect_assessments.scope: The apocynin incubation arm of the U46619 readout.

findings.description: n08 asserts that TXA2 induces hypercontractility in exposed aortas and that the response is associated with oxidative stress and reversed by apocynin. o09 reports the higher Emax of U46619 contraction in exposed animals versus CTRL, while o11 and o12 show that the response is reduced by apocynin in 80 ppm rings and that the apocynin-normalised 40 ppm response does not differ from CTRL. These observations support a functional response to U46619 and apocynin attenuation of it, rather than a direct measurement of TXA2 receptor number, TXA2 production or downstream signalling. The map already contains the interpretation claim n12, so the useful change is a refinement edge from n08 to n12 rather than a new aspect.
The apocynin arm was run for rings from animals exposed to 80 ppm, as shown by o12, so n07 should carry that comparator rather than leave it unspecified.

proposed_updates.rationale: The existing claim n12 already states that the hypercontractile responses should be interpreted as increased functional responsiveness rather than definitive proof of enhanced TXA2 signalling or receptor upregulation and that they do not establish a direct causal role for TXA2 in hypertension. The useful change is to link n08 to n12 as a refinement, so that the interpretation is attached to the claim that asserts the TXA2-induced hypercontractility rather than being a separate aspect. This preserves the two statements and their evidence while checking that the stronger claim is supported by the apocynin readouts.

verification_needs.why_informative: If the apocynin effect is reduced or absent in Cd2+ 80 ppm rings preincubated with SQ29548, it would support a TXA2 receptor-mediated component of the response; if it persists, the apocynin effect would be attributable to a non-specific reduction in contractility or to another pathway.

needed_observations: TXA2 receptor number in aortic homogenates

The claim's statement about IL confinement is also not supported by any visible observation. The correct action is therefore to restate cl01 as a qualitative observation of no new XRD peaks after IL incorporation, and to retain the hard-phase SAXS shift and the tensile comparison (o15) as separate evidence.

The induced phenotype must be attributable to the keratin moiety rather than to the fusion tag used to express it.
Whether the antigen-specific disease obtained in BALB/c mice can be generalized to another mouse genetic background must be determined.
The immunogens and their tag-only counterparts must be produced with verified identity, assessed purity and controlled endotoxin before immunization.

The evidence is the same FTIR/XPS/elemental analysis, so the two aspects ask different questions and should remain separate. a42 is dynamic dipole–dipole interactions among the side chains. Its evidence is the same temperature-dependent FTIR (o02), so it is a structural/interaction aspect of the same modification. a43 is ion–dipole interactions between the side chains and the IL, addressed by e02 with FTIR and XPS of neat IL, i-PMPU@30% and ZESTI@30%. The redshifts in ZESTI and the S 2p/N 1s changes are relevant, but they do not isolate the zwitterion–IL interaction: the redshifts can be due to the IL interacting with the host polymer (i-PMPU@30%) or with the polymer network, and the XPS shifts depend on the IL and the host. So a43 needs its own aspect. The organization is correct, and no consolidation is warranted. The remaining question is how to distinguish the zwitterion–IL interaction from the host–IL interaction.
</think>

aspect_assessments.assessment: The visible evidence supports the attribution of the clinical and immunological readouts to the keratin antigen rather than to the fusion tag.
limitations: The adjuvant control group is not reported with outcomes in the retrieved text.
The negative serum used for the ELISA ratio is not specified.
The GST and TF tag-only groups were not reported with outcomes.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The comparison groups differ only in antigen, and the visible readouts move with the antigen rather than the tag.
aspect_assessments.scope: Female BALB/c and C57BL/6J mice, two GST-tagged and three TF-tagged series, 5-10 mice per group.

aspect_assessments.assessment: K14 and K17 differ in the visible readouts: 4/10 versus 7/10 BALB/c mice showed symptoms after primary immunization, and the TF-K14 group showed symptoms on day 8 while the TF-K17 group did so on day 11.
limitations: Symptom counts are not given for the GST or TF control groups.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The difference is between antigens, and the visible readouts are consistent with an antigen-specific effect.
aspect_assessments.scope: BALB/c mice, primary immunization.

aspect_assessments.assessment: IgM titers and IgG1/IgG2b titers exceeded the specified threshold after immunization with both K14 and K17.
limitations: No titers for the control groups are visible.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The visible titers are higher in antigen-immunized mice, which is consistent with the antigen being the target of the response.
aspect_assessments.scope: BALB/c mice, 7, 14, 21 and 24 days after immunization.

aspect_assessments.assessment: Lymph node and spleen cells from K14/K17-immunized mice release more IFN-gamma after antigen restimulation than cells from control mice.
limitations: No T-cell subset or cytokine-panel readout is visible.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The cytokine response moves with the antigen rather than the tag.
aspect_assessments.scope: BALB/c and C57BL/6J mice, 7 and 10 days after booster immunization.

aspect_assessments.assessment: The claim that the phenotype is attributable to the keratin moiety is supported by the sequence identity of the tags with K14, by the similar results obtained with the two different fusion-tag systems, and by the comparison groups differing only in antigen.
limitations: The adjuvant control group is not reported with outcomes in the retrieved text.
The visible readouts do not exclude a contribution of the tag.
aspect_assessments.rationale: The evidence is the same as the evidence cited in the claim, and the claim is worded at the scope of the visible comparison groups.
aspect_assessments.scope: K14 and K17 fusion proteins compared with the same adjuvant, in female BALB/c and C57BL/6J mice.

findings.description: The visible readouts are consistent with the antigen being the cause of the responses, but they are also consistent with the fusion tag being the cause.
The visible incidence difference is between K14 and K17, not between GST and TF antigen.
The visible lesion-onset difference is between the two GST-tagged groups, not between GST and TF antigen.
Tag removal during purification caused substantial protein loss, so the visible tag-only groups were not reported with outcomes.

information_requests: The outcome of the adjuvant-only group in the GST-tagged series, since the visible readouts do not separate the effect of the antigen from the effect of the adjuvant.

add_nodes.statement: The clinical and immunological outcomes are attributable to the fusion tag rather than to the keratin antigen; the low sequence identity of the GST and TF tags with K14 (3.93% and 4.5%) and the similar results obtained with the two different fusion-tag systems support this alternative, and the visible readouts are compatible with it.

proposed_updates.rationale: The visible readouts are compatible with the tag explanation, so it is a candidate explanation rather than a verified finding. The alternative is added as a proposal, and its distinguishing test is the tag-only group with the same adjuvant.

n13 says the lower cardiac superoxide in transplanted MI rats appears independent of antioxidant defense because SOD1/SOD2 mRNA did not change. That is a candidate explanation, not a measurement. o15 reports no changes in SOD1 or SOD2 mRNA in any of the four groups, including MI + mitochondria, which is what SOD1/SOD2 mRNA does not change. But the DHE signal is a red-fluorescent product of superoxide, not a measurement of superoxide itself; it also reports no mitochondrial protein in the injection (e06), so the donor mitochondria are not measured. The experiment does not compare transplanted hearts with sham hearts receiving mitochondria, so n13 cannot be tested by a within-group comparison. A candidate alternative is therefore that lower superoxide reflects less mitochondrial superoxide production, perhaps from a lower number of functional donor mitochondria in MI + mitochondria hearts, because the dose is fixed at 180 μg mitochondrial protein in 75 μL, and MI hearts are less viable than sham hearts. The alternative is linked to n13 as a competing explanation. A distinguishing comparison is a within-group mitochondrial protein measurement and an MI vs sham comparison of mitochondrial superoxide production in hearts receiving mitochondria at the same dose, with SOD1/SOD2 mRNA measured in parallel.
</think>

The EPR signal is an oxygen-vacancy probe of the perovskite (o41) and the XRD shows no Al phases (o13), so the vacancies are in the perovskite. The vacancy-channel explanation in i06 says the vacancies are O2− migration channels that let CO2 cross the CaCO3 layer and react with inner CaO. That would mean the faster k1 and k2 come from faster O2− transport across CaCO3, and the linear relation in o37 would be the channel density versus k. The alternative is that the vacancies are on the surface of the CaO, where they speed CO2 adsorption and the linear relation is the surface vacancy concentration versus k. The two differ in where the vacancies act and what the rate-limiting step is. The perovskite has a high Ov signal (o41), and the DFMs have extra CaCO3 peaks (o35), so both are plausible. The test is whether the rate changes when the perovskite is absent. If the LaNi0.8Al0.2O3/CaO DFM and a CaO-only DFM have similar k1 and k2, the vacancies must be on CaO; if the DFMs still have faster k1 and k2, the vacancies are in the perovskite and the channel explanation is supported.

findings.description: The faster CO2 uptake of the Al-doped DFMs could come from vacancies on the CaO surface speeding CO2 adsorption, which would make the linear relation of k1 and k2 with the EPR Ov signal a surface-vacancy concentration effect, rather than from O2− migration channels through CaCO3.

add_nodes.statement: Surface oxygen vacancies in CaO, created by Al doping of the perovskite, increase the CO2 adsorption rate on the CaO surface, so the faster CO2 uptake of the Al-doped DFMs at 650 °C comes from faster CO2 adsorption on CaO rather than from O2− migration channels through the CaCO3 layer.

findings.description: The objective contains multiple distinct questions that require different measurements.

add_nodes.statement: The pre-sodiation step improves the initial coulombic efficiency of the anode and compensates the active Na+ lost during first-cycle SEI formation.
The pre-sodiation step is ex situ and does not evolve gas or cause electrode swelling.
The pre-sodiation step can be carried out on a continuous, large-area (roll-to-roll) electrode production line.
The pre-sodiation step increases the anode's initial coulombic efficiency within minutes.
The pre-sodiation step does not add Na+ beyond the amount lost during first-cycle SEI formation; the added Na+ remains in the anode during cycling.
Dehydration of the hydrothermal CaV8O20·nH2O precursor by annealing preserves the layered vanadate framework and its interlayer spacing.
The dehydrated anode stores Na+ reversibly with stable long-term half-cell cycling, with Ca2+ remaining redox-inactive and the lattice changing only slightly during sodiation.
The dehydrated anode's Na+ storage kinetics are fast enough to match the kinetics of a capacitive cathode in a sodium-ion capacitor.
A sodium-ion capacitor built with the pre-sodiated anode delivers high specific energy and power together with long cycle life.

The public packet contains a claim about APTES converting inert SiC into a well-dispersed filler that improves rheology, contact and interfacial resistance. The available observations address each part: o01-o07 show SiC-APTES attached to SiC and present in the electrode, o08-o09 compare the two additive types across loadings, o10-o12 compare device performance at each additive's optimal loading, o21 shows cross-sectional contact, and o24 compares interfacial conductivity. The most informative next step is therefore a controlled experiment that varies APTES while holding SiC fixed. The packet already contains the functionalization step, so I suggest varying the APTES-to-SiC ratio during that step and measuring the same rheology, contact and device endpoints. I do not assert that the ratio effect is already known, because the packet does not contain a design that varies the ratio.
</think>
